name: Evidence Extraction Tables
title: Evidence Extraction Tables
answer: An evidence extraction table is a structured grid that records, for each study in a review, the specific pieces of information the reviewers need: study design, population, intervention or exposure, comparator, outcomes measured, results, and any risk of bias judgement. It sits inside systematic review and evidence synthesis work, where it turns a pile of full texts into a comparable dataset that later feeds a narrative summary or a meta analysis. The table is not a summary of each paper in prose, it is a set of fields with one row per study and one column per question the review protocol asks. Its scope is fixed by the protocol before extraction starts, so the table answers the review question rather than whatever happens to be interesting in a given paper.

sections.body: An evidence extraction table is a structured grid that records, for each study in a review, the specific pieces of information the reviewers need: study design, population, intervention or exposure, comparator, outcomes measured, results, and any risk of bias judgement. It sits inside systematic review and evidence synthesis work, where it turns a pile of full texts into a comparable dataset that later feeds a narrative summary or a meta analysis. The table is not a summary of each paper in prose, it is a set of fields with one row per study and one column per question the review protocol asks. Its scope is fixed by the protocol before extraction starts, so the table answers the review question rather than whatever happens to be interesting in a given paper.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Most extraction tables live in a spreadsheet, a reference manager with a data extraction module, or a dedicated systematic review platform, and the choice usually follows what the team already uses for screening and deduplication. The table itself is a file, often shared, versioned, and locked once the team agrees on the field list. Behind it sit the full texts, the protocol, the search strategy, and the screening decisions, all of which need to stay linked so a reviewer can trace any cell back to the sentence it came from. Where the review is large, the table may be split by outcome or by study design and recombined at analysis, and the infrastructure has to keep those pieces consistent.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Extraction usually starts with a pilot on a small set of studies, where two reviewers fill the table independently and then compare, so ambiguous fields get sharpened before the bulk of the work. After that, each study is extracted by one reviewer and checked by a second, or by two reviewers working independently with disagreements resolved by discussion or a third party. Fields are defined in a codebook that says exactly what counts as, for example, the primary outcome or the follow up period, and any deviation is logged. Reviewers often paste the supporting quotation into a notes column so the judgement can be audited later, and the completed table is the input to risk of bias assessment and to any synthesis.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The main risks are extraction error, selective extraction of favourable results, and loss of the link between a cell and its source, so reviews commonly keep a notes column, a codebook, and a record of who extracted what and when. Provenance matters because a reader may want to check a number against the original paper, and because updates to a living review need to know which cells changed and why. Copyright and licensing constrain how much verbatim text can be stored in a shared table, and personal data from study participants should not be copied into a working file that is not needed for the analysis. Where the review informs guidance or policy, the extraction table is often part of what gets published or deposited, so it has to be intelligible to someone who was not on the team.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Machine learning and language models are increasingly used to pre fill candidate cells or to flag studies for a second look, but the reviewer still owns the judgement and the codebook still has to define the field. The direction of travel is toward tables that are machine readable from the start, with controlled vocabularies and stable identifiers for studies, outcomes, and populations, so that evidence can be pooled across reviews rather than rebuilt each time. Living reviews and rapid updates put pressure on extraction to be faster without becoming less traceable, which tends to push teams toward clearer field definitions and better audit trails rather than toward removing the human check. The table is likely to remain the point where a review's question meets its evidence, whatever tool is used to fill it.
